lesson.title: Reading the Downhill Reaction: Exothermic Energy Diagrams
lesson.summary: Exothermic reactions release energy to the surroundings, and a reaction coordinate diagram shows this as products ending up lower in potential energy than the reactants.
lesson.body:
A reaction coordinate diagram plots potential energy on the vertical axis against reaction progress on the horizontal axis. Every reaction has to climb an energy hill before it can turn into products, and the height of that hill, measured from the reactants up to its peak, is the activation energy, Ea. What makes a diagram exothermic is not the hill itself but where the curve lands when it comes back down.

In an exothermic reaction, the products end up lower on the energy axis than the reactants started. Picture the reactants drawn on the left at some starting height. The curve rises to a peak, labeled the transition state or activated complex, and the vertical distance from the reactants up to that peak is Ea for the forward reaction. The curve then drops, not just back to the starting height but below it, ending at the products, drawn lower on the diagram. The vertical drop from reactants down to products is the enthalpy change, delta H, and for an exothermic reaction that value is negative because energy left the system and went into the surroundings as heat. Notice also that the reverse reaction, read right to left, has to climb from the low products back up to the same peak, so Ea for the reverse direction is larger than Ea for the forward direction. That asymmetry, a short climb one way and a long climb the other, is the signature of an exothermic diagram.

A concrete example makes this precise. The combustion of methane, CH4 + 2O2 producing CO2 + 2H2O, releases roughly 890 kJ for every mole of methane burned, so delta H is about negative 890 kJ per mole. On the diagram, the reactants CH4 and O2 start relatively high. The curve climbs a modest hill, Ea forward, up to a transition state where old bonds are partway broken and new bonds are partway formed, then falls sharply down to the products CO2 and water, which sit far below where the reactants began. That large drop is exactly what gets released as heat, which is why combustion can warm a room or drive an engine.

This connects directly to what you already know about exothermic reactions from a bonding standpoint: more energy is released forming the new bonds in the products than was required to break the bonds in the reactants, and that surplus leaves as heat. It is worth keeping delta H and Ea conceptually separate even though they both live on the same diagram. Delta H is thermodynamic: it only compares where you started to where you ended. Ea is kinetic: it describes how tall a barrier stands in between. A reaction can be strongly exothermic, a big drop from reactants to products, and still be very slow if that middle barrier is tall. Methane and oxygen, for instance, can sit together at room temperature almost indefinitely without reacting, even though the reaction is enormously exothermic, because Ea is high enough that a spark or flame is needed to get enough molecules over the hill.
